extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policymakers, regulatory agencies (FSOC/OIRA), and regulatory reform advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and designing institutional procedures for cost-benefit analysis, interagency coordination, and review of financial regulatory rulemaking (e.g., FSOC, OIRA interactions). Focuses on improving analytical rigor, transparency, and collaboration across financial regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal coordination policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish formal collaboration and coordination policies (GAO recommended the FSOC “to strengthen accountability and collaboration,” including creating “formal collaboration and coordination policies”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of coordination practices include coordinating member agency rulemaking timelines, performing collaborative systemwide stress tests, forming external advisory committees, and establishing clear roles to avoid duplication, confusion, and regulatory gaps. GAO emphasized that coordination can respect member autonomy while improving outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal cost-benefit analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Execute formal cost-benefit analyses for financial regulation (advocated by Bipartisan Policy Center and recommended by GAO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FSOC could promote execution of formal CBA across member agencies and better ensure incorporation of OMB/OMB Circular A-4 practices into rulemakings. The Center for Capital Markets also advocates formal cost-benefit analyses as part of FSOC's coordinating responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate staffing and analytical expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure sufficient staff and analytical capacity to perform coordination and high-quality regulatory analysis (FSOC budgeted 36 positions but likely needs more to bolster analytical capabilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FSOC should recruit economists, lawyers, policy professionals, and others with private- and public-sector experience. Comparative benchmarking: EPA’s Office of Policy employs roughly 140 FTEs, suggesting FSOC may need substantially more staff to serve as a clearinghouse and provide crosscutting analytical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent, open process with meaningful public participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a consistent, transparent, and open process that provides ample opportunities for public comment (modeled by the Interagency Working Group on the Social Cost of Carbon (IWG)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish technical support documents detailing decisionmaking and model use, solicit public comments, respond substantively to comments (IWG received many submissions and published a 44-page response), and allow agency-level notice-and-comment on rules that use the estimate. Transparency and responsiveness to stakeholders are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust uncertainty analysis and protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and follow protocols for handling deep uncertainty (IWG used Monte Carlo analysis to address long-term climate uncertainty, climate sensitivity, discount rates, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate statistical techniques (e.g., Monte Carlo), explicitly document assumptions (e.g., climate sensitivity, discounting in intergenerational contexts), and create a protocol for treating uncertainty so analysis is consistent and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external peer review and scientific updating
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject modeling and economic assumptions to external scientific review and update estimates based on the latest research (IWG asked the National Academy of Sciences to review modeling approaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage external expert bodies (e.g., NAS) to review methods and incorporate updated research into regulatory impact analyses to improve credibility and technical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish technical documentation and respond to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Document analytic methods in Technical Support Documents and produce substantive responses to public comments (IWG published TSDs and a 44-page response to comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed documentation helps stakeholders evaluate methods and assumptions; coordinating bodies should publish both methods and dispositions of comments to demonstrate rigor and openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote regulatory efficiency and reduce duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor and mitigate cumulative regulatory impacts, identify and fill regulatory gaps, and streamline duplicative regulations, reporting, and oversight (recommended for FSOC by Center for Capital Markets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use FSOC’s coordinating role to detect overlap and inconsistencies across member agencies and to take steps that reduce unnecessary burdens while addressing systemic risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination that respects agency autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement coordination practices while respecting statutory autonomy of member agencies (FSOC cited lack of statutory authority as limiting its actions; GAO argued coordination was still possible without infringing autonomy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design coordination tools that provide systemwide perspectives and analytical support but stop short of usurping substantive policymaking authority of individual agencies; emphasize indirect/technical coordination (MOUs, clearinghouse functions) rather than command-and-control measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use MOUs and clearinghouse functions to diffuse expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: FSOC could enter into memoranda of understanding and serve as a clearinghouse to broker analytical synergies and diffuse expertise among member agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical unilateral steps include MOUs with individual agencies, offering systemic outlooks and analytical firepower to member agency rulemakings, and centralizing specialized analytic capacity to support complex inter-agency rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend OIRA review to independent agencies (subject to legal/political considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider empowering OIRA to review regulatory analysis of independent agencies to harmonize practices and improve rigor and transparency (legal and political arguments suggest the President can extend such review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits cited include diffusion of OIRA expertise, harmonization of methods, and increased rigor; constraints include possible congressional backlash and legal questions about presidential authority. Legislative proposals (e.g., Independent Agency Regulatory Analysis Act) and letters from former OIRA administrators argue for extension, but implementation requires attention to political feasibility and agency-specific concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplicative review to prevent cost and delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh tradeoffs of sequential FSOC and OIRA review—duplicate review risks needless cost and delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer using OIRA to build FSOC capacity so that at a later point FSOC-coordinated analyses might be exempted from OIRA review; design review sequencing to minimize redundancy while ensuring quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonize methodological approaches across agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve conflicts between differing efficiency or evaluation criteria used by agencies (e.g., SEC’s 'investor welfare approach' vs OMB’s 'total surplus approach') before imposing unified review regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize addressing fundamental methodological dissonance across agencies so that extending a single review standard (like OIRA's) does not impose incompatible metrics; studies and prior work should identify and resolve these conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt cost-benefit analysis for multi-member agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and adjust for institutional differences: multi-member, bipartisan commissions may operate differently from hierarchical single-head agencies, affecting how economic analysis informs decisions (Kraus & Raso argue CBA plays a different role in multi-member bodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design analytic processes that inform deliberation and compromise in multimember settings rather than assuming hierarchical flows; nevertheless, judicial trends may require increased analytical transparency and rigor regardless of internal decision structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional arguments support institutional design choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use functional/pragmatic considerations (e.g., improving outcomes, diffusion of expertise) alongside structural and constitutional analysis when judging the desirability of extending review or reorganizing oversight (cites Posner, Choper, Chemerinsky).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy design should weigh practical consequences—such as whether OIRA review will improve analytic quality—along with legal feasibility, and align structural changes with demonstrable functional benefits.
